facts.claim: 'Restlessness' is a single by Benjamin Haycock, released 8 January 2021, running 2:42.
Deezer's credits list Benjamin Haycock as both writer and composer of 'Restlessness'.
The song appears on the single and also on the 2021 EP 'Enigma's Quay'.
Bandcamp tags the track as alternative hip-hop, acoustic rap, alternative folk, percussive guitar and singer-songwriter, and lists the UK as its origin.
Haycock performed 'Restlessness' at his blind audition on The Voice UK. All four coaches turned, and he chose will.i.am's team.
Haycock told the judges the song is addressed to his late father. It speaks about the things people battle with in their minds and keep inside.
The Music Man describes the song as a percussive guitar piece that mixes pop, rap and grit, with a stripped-back, Bob Dylan-style authenticity.
Haycock is from Birmingham, England, and was born on 17 February 1996.
His debut release 'Uprooted Alone' is about leaving the place where he grew up and lost his father, and the loneliness of moving to a new home.

He is a singer-songwriter, multi-instrumentalist, rapper and producer. After losing his father he moved to the Devon coast, and the Tree Council's Young Tree Champions programme lists him as an ambassador.

research.lineage: It sits in the UK singer-songwriter tradition of acoustic folk mixed with rap, built on percussive guitar playing and confessional lyrics.

draft:
The second verse of **Restlessness** opens like a phone call home: "Dad, I've found love now." Then comes the news anyone would want to share: the move to the coast, the hair grown out and gone curly. Benjamin Haycock wrote the song to his late father, and the heartbreak is in how ordinary these updates are. He is giving a report to someone who can't answer, and the pride in it is real.

The line that catches is "And apparently, I'm looking more like you every day." The word "apparently" carries it. Someone else told him. He is hearing about his own resemblance second-hand and carrying it like a gift and a wound at once. Growing into a father's face is how the dead stay close, and it is also a daily reminder of who is missing. The song doesn't choose between those feelings. Out on the water, between waves, it lands on "Of the ocean's the place I can hear you talk, Dad." Haycock moved to the Devon coast after his father died, so the sea in the song is both the new home and the place where the conversation carries on.

The chorus pulls back from the private letter to a shared one. Its minds are "our" minds, its scars are ones time won't remove, and its fighters are dug into trenches against their own past. Haycock has said the song is about what people battle in their heads and keep inside. The chorus enacts that. Each time it reaches its title phrase it breaks off, once into a hum, and the last time it simply stops mid-word. The restlessness never finishes its sentence.

Between those passages Haycock raps. One verse stacks short, hard vowel sounds into a dense run where momentum outpaces meaning, which is its own way of saying the head won't quiet down. Bandcamp files the track under acoustic rap and alternative folk with percussive guitar, and the song sits in that UK strand of confessional folk with bars folded in. The Music Man called it pop, rap and grit with a stripped-back, Dylan-style plainness. Rapid speech gives way to a low, slightly rough, breathy singing voice that holds its notes with a little vibrato. A clean, arpeggiated guitar keeps a slow, relaxed pace. Voice and guitar each get their own space in a natural-sounding room, and nothing builds. It's the song Haycock brought to his blind audition on The Voice UK, where all four coaches turned.

What sticks is the casual "apparently," the sound of someone finding out from other people's faces that a parent is still alive in theirs.

factCheck.note: The chorus's closing line breaks off all three times. Twice it goes into 'mmm-mm' and the third time it ends on 'restlessness of our-'. The first part of the chorus is not cut off, and the hum happens twice, not once.

factCheck.note: Rap is supported by the Bandcamp tags and The Music Man. 'Short, hard vowel sounds' is not backed by the lyrics, so it was replaced with the actual vocabulary of the verse ('sediments', 'embezzling', 'benevolence').
